Deep-dive EDA: price patterns in the four day-ahead zones¶

What this notebook answers: when are prices high and low, how they move hour by hour, across weekdays and seasons, how the four zones relate to each other, and what happens inside each hour (the 15-minute shape we have to reconstruct).

Data: Data/train_prices_15min.csv only (no external data). Prices are day-ahead prices in EUR/MWh, not consumption. The data contains no load figures, but price follows demand minus cheap supply (mostly solar and wind), so the patterns below are the market's reading of "energy usage".

Window: 2025-10-01 → 2026-08-31 (333 days per zone). September 2026 stays out, as in the team's initial_analysis.py, so it can serve as an untouched final holdout.

Notation: H = hourly price (mean of the 4 quarters). res = price − H, the intra-hour deviation; the four res values of an hour sum to zero.

In [1]:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, matplotlib as mpl
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
from pathlib import Path

DATA = Path('../Data/train_prices_15min.csv')
FIG = Path('results/eda_deep_dive'); FIG.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
EDA_END = '2026-08-31'

ZONES = ['ZONE_0', 'ZONE_1', 'ZONE_2', 'ZONE_3']
ZC = dict(zip(ZONES, ['#2a78d6', '#eb6834', '#1baf7a', '#eda100']))   # fixed colour per zone
SEQ = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list('seq', ['#f3f6fb', '#9ec3ee', '#2a78d6', '#0d3a73'])
DIV = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list('div', ['#2a78d6', '#e9e8e4', '#e34948'])
mpl.rcParams.update({'figure.dpi': 110, 'axes.spines.top': False, 'axes.spines.right': False,
                     'axes.grid': True, 'grid.color': '#e6e6e3', 'grid.linewidth': .6,
                     'axes.edgecolor': '#9a9994', 'axes.titleweight': 'bold', 'axes.titlesize': 11,
                     'font.size': 9, 'lines.linewidth': 2, 'legend.frameon': False})
def save(fig, name): fig.savefig(FIG / f'{name}.png', bbox_inches='tight', dpi=130)

raw = pd.read_csv(DATA, parse_dates=['delivery_date'])
df = raw[raw.delivery_date <= EDA_END].copy()
df['H'] = df.groupby(['delivery_date', 'market_id', 'hour_index']).price_eur_mwh.transform('mean')
df['res'] = df.price_eur_mwh - df.H
df['dow'] = df.delivery_date.dt.dayofweek
df['weekend'] = df.dow >= 5
df['month'] = df.delivery_date.dt.month
df['ym'] = df.delivery_date.dt.to_period('M')
SEASON = {12:'Winter',1:'Winter',2:'Winter',3:'Spring',4:'Spring',5:'Spring',6:'Summer',7:'Summer',8:'Summer',9:'Autumn',10:'Autumn',11:'Autumn'}
df['season'] = df.month.map(SEASON)

# one row per (zone, day, hour)
hr = (df.groupby(['market_id', 'delivery_date', 'hour_index'])
        .agg(H=('H', 'first'), q1=('price_eur_mwh', 'first'), q4=('price_eur_mwh', 'last'),
             mad=('res', lambda s: s.abs().mean()))
        .reset_index())
hr['tilt'] = hr.q4 - hr.q1
for c in ['dow', 'month', 'season', 'weekend']:
    hr[c] = hr.delivery_date.map(df.drop_duplicates('delivery_date').set_index('delivery_date')[c])
print(f'{len(df):,} quarter-hour rows · {df.delivery_date.nunique()} days · {df.market_id.nunique()} zones')

127,872 quarter-hour rows · 333 days · 4 zones

1. Price levels and distributions¶

What we found: levels

  • ZONE_2 is the expensive, calm zone (mean 132 €, std 37, never below 0 €). ZONE_3 is the cheapest and most volatile relative to its level (mean 71 €, 6.6 % of quarter-hours negative, ~10 % at or below zero).
  • ZONE_0 and ZONE_1 sit in between (101 € and 115 €) but have the fattest tails: −500 € to +747 € (ZONE_0) and −499 € to +645 € (ZONE_1).
  • The negative floor (≈ −500 €) is hit on a single day, 1 May 2026 (public holiday + strong solar), at the same hours in ZONE_0, ZONE_1 and ZONE_3, so these three markets are coupled.
  • The distributions have a long right tail and a small negative cluster. Use robust statistics (median, MAE, Spearman). Averages and Pearson correlations are pulled by a handful of days.

# Profiles by season: the duck curve deepens in spring/summer
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.4), sharey=True)
order = ['Autumn', 'Winter', 'Spring', 'Summer']
for ax, z in zip(axs, ZONES):
    s = hr[hr.market_id == z].groupby(['season', 'hour_index']).H.mean().unstack(0)[order]
    for i, se in enumerate(order):
        ax.plot(s.index, s[se], color=['#c3c2b7', '#6f6e69', '#7fb3ea', '#0d3a73'][i], label=se)
    ax.set(title=z, xticks=[1, 6, 12, 18, 24], xlabel='hour')
axs[0].set_ylabel('mean hourly price, EUR/MWh'); axs[0].legend()
fig.suptitle('Daily profile by season: the midday solar trough deepens from spring on', fontweight='bold', y=1.03)
save(fig, '03_profile_by_season'); plt.show()

# Hour × month heatmaps of the mean price
months = sorted(hr.delivery_date.dt.to_period('M').unique())
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 4.2), sharey=True)
for ax, z in zip(axs, ZONES):
    m = hr[hr.market_id == z].assign(ym=lambda d: d.delivery_date.dt.to_period('M')).pivot_table(index='hour_index', columns='ym', values='H')
    im = ax.imshow(m.values, aspect='auto', cmap=SEQ, origin='lower', extent=[-.5, m.shape[1] - .5, .5, 24.5])
    ax.set(title=z, xticks=range(m.shape[1]), yticks=[1, 6, 12, 18, 24])
    ax.set_xticklabels([p.strftime('%b') for p in m.columns], rotation=90); ax.grid(False)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=.046, pad=.02)
axs[0].set_ylabel('hour_index'); fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=.35)
fig.suptitle('Mean hourly price by month and hour (EUR/MWh; each zone has its own colour scale)', fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
save(fig, '04_hour_month_heatmap'); plt.show()

What we found: hourly trends

  • All four zones follow the same "duck curve": a morning peak at hour 8 (07–08h), a deep midday trough at hour 14 (13–14h) and the daily maximum in the evening, hour 20–21 (19–21h). The night (hours 2–5) is a flat, medium-price plateau.
  • The trough depth differs by zone: evening peak / midday low ≈ 3.9× in ZONE_3, 3.0× in ZONE_0, 2.4× in ZONE_1, but only 1.6× in ZONE_2. ZONE_2 has the least solar-driven price structure.
  • Season changes the shape a lot. In autumn and winter the midday dip is shallow and the day has two humps (morning and evening, e.g. ZONE_0 hour 13 ≈ 95 € in winter). From March the midday price collapses (ZONE_0 hour 13 ≈ 16 € in spring, ZONE_3 ≈ 6 €) and the evening peak grows (ZONE_0 hour 21 ≈ 203 € in summer).
  • The month × hour heatmaps show the trough appearing in March–April (deepest in April/May) and August as the most expensive month in every zone, mostly through the evening hours. January is the high month of the winter.

What we found: weekly pattern

  • Weekends are 25–26 % cheaper in ZONE_0, ZONE_1 and ZONE_3, and 13 % cheaper in ZONE_2. Sunday is the cheapest day everywhere; Tuesday/Wednesday are the most expensive.
  • The discount depends on the hour. It is ~0 % at night (hours 1–5), grows through the morning (25 % at hour 7) and is largest at midday, hours 11–16: 50–60 % in ZONE_0/1, up to 72 % in ZONE_3, ~35 % in ZONE_2. Lower business demand meets the same solar supply. The evening peak shrinks only 15–20 %.
  • Monday morning and Friday evening sit between the two regimes, so a weekday/weekend flag is the minimum calendar feature. Day-of-week is better.

# Monthly trend of level and daily spread
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.6))
for z in ZONES:
    d = daily[daily.market_id == z].set_index('delivery_date')
    axs[0].plot(d.dmean.rolling(14, center=True).mean(), color=ZC[z], label=z)
    axs[1].plot(d.spread.rolling(14, center=True).mean(), color=ZC[z], label=z)
axs[0].set(title='Daily mean price (14-day rolling)', ylabel='EUR/MWh'); axs[1].set(title='Daily spread = max − min hourly price (14-day rolling)', ylabel='EUR/MWh')
axs[0].legend(ncol=4)
for a in axs: a.tick_params(axis='x', rotation=30)
save(fig, '08_trend_level_spread'); plt.show()

What we found: peaks and lows

  • Daily peak timing is seasonal. In Oct–Feb the peak is at hours 18–20 (early winter sunset), with a secondary cluster at hour 9 (morning peak wins on some days). In Mar–Aug the peak moves to hour 21 for ZONE_0/1/2 (≈ 45 % of days) and hours 20–23 for ZONE_3.
  • Daily low timing switches regime. In winter the low is at night (hours 3–5) or at hour 24. In spring/summer it is at midday (hours 13–15), the solar trough (ZONE_3: hour 14 on ~60 % of days).
  • Negative prices are a solar-midday phenomenon: concentrated at hours 11–17, March–August, peaking in April, when 50–60 % of 13–15h quarter-hours are negative in ZONE_0 and ZONE_3. ZONE_2 never goes negative. There is a small night-time negative episode in October 2025 in ZONE_0/ZONE_3 (windy nights).
  • Extreme spikes cluster on a few days: 24 June 2026 (hours 20–21, up to 747 € in ZONE_0) and 12–13 August 2026 (hour 20, up to 487 € in ZONE_3). Spikes almost always fall on the last quarter (Q4) of evening hours 20–21, so spikes have an intra-hour shape too.
  • Daily spread (max − min hourly price) is largest in ZONE_0 (median 127 €) and smallest in ZONE_2 (66 €). It grows from spring on, along with the solar trough.

5. Volatility: which hours are hardest to predict?¶

In [11]:
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.6))
for z in ZONES:
    h = hr[hr.market_id == z]
    axs[0].plot(h.groupby('hour_index').H.std(), color=ZC[z], label=z)
    axs[1].plot(h.groupby('hour_index').mad.mean(), color=ZC[z], label=z)
axs[0].set(title='Day-to-day std of the hourly price, by hour', ylabel='EUR/MWh', xticks=[1, 6, 12, 18, 24], xlabel='hour')
axs[1].set(title='Intra-hour movement: mean |price − hourly mean| (= flat-baseline MAE)', ylabel='EUR/MWh', xticks=[1, 6, 12, 18, 24], xlabel='hour')
axs[0].legend(ncol=2)
save(fig, '09_volatility_by_hour'); plt.show()

What we found: volatility

  • Day-to-day uncertainty of the hourly price is highest at midday (hours 13–15, std up to 74 €) and around hour 21. These are the hours that depend on solar output and on the evening ramp.
  • Intra-hour movement (what we reconstruct) peaks on the ramps, not at the price peaks. It has two humps: the morning peak / solar down-ramp (hours 8–10, 12–14 € in ZONE_0/1) and the evening up-ramp (hours 17–20, up to 17 € in ZONE_1). It is lowest at night (hours 3–5, ≈ 2 €) and at the bottom of the midday trough (hours 13–14, ≈ 3–4 €).
  • So the hours with the most to gain over the flat baseline are the ramp hours, where neighbouring hourly prices differ a lot.

6c. What drives the intra-hour shape? Correlation with features known at inference¶

In [14]:
hr = hr.sort_values(['market_id', 'delivery_date', 'hour_index']).reset_index(drop=True)
g = hr.groupby(['market_id', 'delivery_date']).H
hr['prev'] = g.shift(1); hr['next'] = g.shift(-1)
hr['slope'] = (hr.next - hr.prev) / 2                     # central slope of the hourly curve
hr['jump_in'] = hr.H - hr.prev; hr['jump_out'] = hr.next - hr.H
hr['curv'] = hr.next - 2 * hr.H + hr.prev
hr['day_mean'] = g.transform('mean'); hr['day_spread'] = g.transform('max') - g.transform('min')
hr['rel_level'] = (hr.H - hr.day_mean) / hr.day_spread.replace(0, np.nan)
# lag: tilt same zone/hour on the previous calendar day (exact-date join, DST gaps respected)
lag = hr[['market_id', 'delivery_date', 'hour_index', 'tilt']].copy(); lag['delivery_date'] += pd.Timedelta(days=1)
hr = hr.merge(lag.rename(columns={'tilt': 'tilt_lag1'}), on=['market_id', 'delivery_date', 'hour_index'], how='left')
feat = ['slope', 'jump_in', 'jump_out', 'curv', 'H', 'rel_level', 'day_spread', 'tilt_lag1']

What we found: correlations

  • Between zones: prices move together (15-min correlation 0.66–0.88). ZONE_0 and ZONE_1 are nearly twins (0.88 for prices, 0.85 for intra-hour deviations). ZONE_2 and ZONE_3 are more independent (residual correlation 0.45–0.61). A model can share structure across zones but should keep zone-specific parameters.
  • Over time: the hourly price has a strong 24-hour rhythm (autocorrelation 0.70–0.78 at lag 24 h). A weekly bump at 168 h is clear in ZONE_2 (0.74 vs 0.68 at 144 h) and ZONE_1 (0.65 vs 0.62), barely visible in ZONE_0/ZONE_3. ZONE_2 is the most persistent and ZONE_0 the least.
  • The direction of the intra-hour ramp is mostly explained by the hourly curve itself: tilt (Q4 − Q1) vs central slope r = 0.91 / 0.86 / 0.76 / 0.82 (ZONE_0…3). A linear fit gives tilt ≈ 1.25–1.83 × slope. Straight-line interpolation between hour centres would give only 0.75 × slope, so the 15-min price moves faster than the hourly curve suggests. Q1 stays near the previous hour and Q4 near the next one (a staircase / sawtooth), so a slope baseline needs a gain of k ≈ 1.7–2.4.
  • Yesterday's tilt at the same hour is the second-best signal (r ≈ 0.62–0.71). It is partly redundant with slope but captures recurring zone-specific shapes.
  • The price level, its position within the day and the day's spread say nothing about direction (r ≈ 0). They correlate weakly with size (0.2–0.36). The size of intra-hour movement relates most to |slope| (Spearman 0.60–0.82).
  • Curvature (next − 2H + prev) is uncorrelated with tilt. It flags local peaks and valleys, where the shape is a "∧" or "∨" rather than a ramp.

# Hour-shape types: ramp (monotonic) vs sawtooth vs other
def shape_type(g):
    d = np.sign(np.diff(g.values))
    if (d == 0).any(): return 'has flat step'
    if (d == d[0]).all(): return 'monotonic ramp'
    if d[0] == d[2] != d[1]: return 'zigzag'
    return 'one turn (peak/valley)'
st = df.sort_values('quarter_index').groupby(['market_id', 'delivery_date', 'hour_index']).price_eur_mwh.apply(shape_type).rename('shape').reset_index()
tab = pd.crosstab(st.market_id, st['shape'], normalize='index').mul(100).round(1)

What we found: inside the hour

  • The outer quarters move, the inner quarters don't. Mean |deviation| is 10–13 € for Q1 and Q4 but only 3–5 € for Q2 and Q3 in every zone. Getting Q1 and Q4 right is most of the score.
  • The hour-by-quarter heatmap shows three regimes:
    • Up-ramps (hours 6–8 morning, 15–20 evening): Q1 below, Q4 above the hourly price.
    • Down-ramps (hours 9–12 solar, 22–24 night): Q1 above, Q4 below.
    • Flat night and midday-trough hours: small shapes. This matches the sign of the hourly slope, which is why the slope is the strongest feature.
  • Most hours are monotonic ramps (72 % in ZONE_0, 68 % in ZONE_1), fewer in ZONE_2/ZONE_3 (≈ 50 %). ZONE_2 has many hours with two equal quarters (25 %): prices often "stick" at the same value. ZONE_3 has the most zigzag / sawtooth hours (19 %).
  • Seasonality of the shape: intra-hour movement is smallest in winter (3.6–6.5 €) and largest in spring/summer (5.9–10.5 €). Weekend shapes are smaller than weekday ones (e.g. ZONE_0 5.7 € vs 8.4 €), except in ZONE_2.
  • The typical-day plots show this: in ZONE_1 and ZONE_3 the 15-min curve oscillates around the flat line within the hour, while in ZONE_2 it follows a smooth staircase.

Summary: what the data tells us¶

Question Answer
When is power most expensive? Evening, hours 20–21 (19–21h), every zone, all year; in winter sometimes hours 18–19 or the morning peak at hour 9.
When is it cheapest? Midday, hour 14 (13–14h) from March to August (solar). In winter, night hours 3–5.
Negative prices? ZONE_3 6.6 %, ZONE_0 5.8 %, ZONE_1 3.1 %, ZONE_2 never. Almost all at 11–17h, Mar–Aug, peaking in April.
Weekly pattern? Weekends ~25 % cheaper (ZONE_2: 13 %), mostly at midday (−50 to −70 %); nights unchanged. Tue/Wed most expensive, Sunday cheapest.
Seasonal pattern? Two-hump winter day → deep "duck curve" spring/summer. August the most expensive month; April has the deepest trough.
How do zones relate? ZONE_0 ≈ ZONE_1 (r 0.88). ZONE_2 calm and high-priced. ZONE_3 cheap, spiky, most negative prices.
Memory? Strong 24 h cycle (r ≈ 0.7–0.78); a weekly echo mainly in ZONE_1/ZONE_2.
What shapes the 15-min profile? The hourly slope (r 0.76–0.91 with Q4−Q1). Then yesterday's shape at the same hour (r 0.62–0.71), then season / weekend / zone for the size.
Where is the error? Q1 and Q4 of ramp hours (morning/solar 8–10, evening 17–20). Night (3–5) and the midday trough (13–14) are easy.

Implications for modelling

  1. Start with a slope-interpolation baseline: residual ≈ k·slope·(−0.375, −0.125, +0.125, +0.375), with k ≈ 1.7–2.4 per zone (fitted tilt ≈ 1.25–1.83 × slope). Plain linear interpolation (k = 1) under-shoots.
  2. Add zone, hour, weekend and season to scale the shape (winter shapes ≈ half of spring/summer).
  3. Add lag features: same hour yesterday and 7 days ago, joined by calendar date so DST gaps do not shift them.
  4. Hours 1 and 24 have only one neighbour; use the one-sided jump there.
  5. Evaluate with MAE and by quarter position. Keep spikes and negative prices in the data, but prefer MAE/L1 losses so they do not dominate.
